docs.title: The map
docs.text:
The Code Index is the module-level map; this table is the edit policy per area.

path what it is how to treat it opencda_marl/ the framework, in four zones: the sealed kernel (_kernel/), the public surface (api/), the plugin system (plugins/), the built-in plugin set (builtin/), plus facades (envs/) and services (telemetry/, evaluation/, utils/, tools/) keep the seams below; the architecture test enforces the zone boundaries opencda_marl/api/ everything third parties import: contracts (policy.py, contracts.py, events.py) and every register_* door public API — a change here updates Add an Algorithm in the same commit and may bump the plugin API version opencda_marl/_kernel/ the complete lifecycle — sealed never imports a plugin; a new behaviour is a registration, never a new if algorithm == …. External code and plugins never import it opencda/ vendored OpenCDA core with local patches every modification is a row in the patch ledger opencda_marl/_bundled/configs/<family>/ default.yaml → <scenario>/base.yaml → profile; the package's own data, shipped in the wheel profiles state only what they change artifacts/_runtime/ per-cell profiles written by the matrix launcher, resolved as an extra config root generated and gitignored — never hand-edit scripts/experiments/ matrix launcher, evaluation launcher, analyzers the experiment-matrix tooling in Run Experiments opencda_marl/_bundled/recordings/*.json deterministic traffic replays evaluation ground truth: changing one invalidates every comparison made on it — do not modify artifacts/, checkpoints/, output/ run outputs (gitignored) possibly someone's only copy — inventory before deleting test/ pytest suites (basic, marl, opencda, route_intent) every change ships with its test docs/ this portal (mkdocs.yml nav is the table of contents; the agent guides in docs/agents/ are built but kept out of the nav) put a feature on the page that owns it; a new topic gets a new page listed in the nav opencda_marl/builtin/algorithms/ the first-party learners; contrib/ inside it is the drop-in folder for cloned-repo algorithms loaded through the wheel's own entry point — engine code never imports a learner module .pixi/, dependencies/whl/ environment and vendored wheels never edit; everything runs through pixi run

docs.title: The seams
docs.text:
These are the invariants that keep the framework pluggable. A change that needs to break one is a design change, and the PR says so.

  • Algorithms do not edit the engine — and the engine imports none. The engine guarantees observation delivery and action application; every learner, the wheel's own builtin/algorithms/ included, arrives through register_algorithm(...) + the opencda_marl.plugins entry point and declares PolicyCapabilities. Dispatch sites read capabilities, never algorithm names or isinstance checks; if a feature needs a name list, the capability is missing — add it.
  • One episode loop for both backends. MARLCoordinator drives CARLA (MARLEnv) and SUMO (SumoMARLEnv) through the same run() / step() / reset_episode() / close(); backend-specific behaviour lives in the environment, not in the coordinator, launcher or monitor.
  • World reloads carry state. TrainingStateSnapshot (in _kernel/lifecycle/world_manager.py) captures and restores learner state across a CARLA world reload. Anything kept on the environment or manager that must survive a reload goes through it.
  • Per-episode state has a home. SUMO: SumoEpisodeState (env.episode). New per-episode fields go there, never as loose attributes with hand-written clears.
  • Observations are str-keyed downstream of the extractor. Raw dicts are keyed by CARLA actor ids (int) or SUMO ids (str); never int(agent_id) — a source-scan test enforces it.
  • Metrics have one sink. Learners log through TrainingLogger (log_scalar / log_episode_metrics), which feeds the metrics store (and TensorBoard when enabled). External policies are covered by MARLManager.record_update_metrics.

docs.title: Commands
docs.text:
pixi run verify                                          # the repeatable battery: suite + registry + components + a real SUMO training run (--full adds CARLA)
pixi run pytest test -q                                  # the whole suite (~5 min, no CARLA needed)
pixi run pytest test/route_intent -q                     # the lifecycle / learner suite
pixi run python -m opencda_marl.plugins            # what is registered, and from where
pixi run python opencda.py -t sumo-marl/intersection/route_speed_only_pcmappo --marl   # SUMO smoke
pixi run marl-quick-test                                 # CARLA smoke (server running)
pixi run -e docs mkdocs build --strict                   # docs must build clean

Tests do not touch CARLA; they skip rather than fail when a GPU lacks headroom. test/conftest.py puts the repo root on sys.path, forces the Agg backend and disables the metrics store — new test files add no path hacks and do not switch the backend; test/opencda/ never gets an __init__.py (it would shadow the real package).

docs.title: Verification duties
docs.text:
A change is done when it is verified, not when it is written. In order of cost:

  1. Unit tests for the change — a new behaviour gets a test that fails without it. Known failures are never "fixed" by weakening assertions.
  2. The suites green on the platform you changed (pixi run pytest test -q). Lifecycle, launcher, config and registry changes are run on both SUMO and CARLA code paths (the tests cover both without a server).
  3. A live smoke run for anything that touches the episode loop, world reloads, the launcher, checkpoints/resume or the monitor: one short SUMO run always; one CARLA run when CARLA code changed. Read the learner's counters (training_step, updates, buffer size) and the monitor, not just the episode summary.
  4. git grep after any move or rename for stale paths — in code, configs, pixi tasks, docs.
  5. Docs in the same commit: a new flag, config key or command appears on the page that owns it (Run Experiments, Add an Algorithm, the Code Index, this page).

Pitfalls that have fooled agents before:

  • Learners whose update() catches exceptions return stale metrics; an isfinite assertion passes on a stale 0.0. Assert that a counter advanced and the loss is non-zero, or read the ERROR log.
  • Bit-identical summaries across two runs of a stochastic learner mean it never acted (a warmup that never ends). Determinism where noise is expected is a failure signal.
  • Seeded outcome numbers are not comparable across commits that change numerics at the ulp level; pin semantics with equivalence tests, not with reward numbers.
  • cProfile inflates tiny functions; device syncs (.item(), .any(), boolean-mask gathers) and gc.collect() are real wall-clock. Microbenchmark before optimising.
  • A failed CUDA-graph capture poisons the process — the feature stays opt-in and fails fast.

docs.title: Commits and pull requests
docs.text:
• Conventional commits, one verified change each: feat(sac): …, fix(launcher): …, perf(envs): …, docs(marl): …, test(route_intent): …, chore(repo): …. The body says what was wrong, what changed, and how it was verified (the command and the observed result).
  • Work on a branch of your fork; open the PR against radar-lab/OpenCDA-MARL main using the PR template. Maintainers review and squash-merge; nobody pushes main directly.

  • Agent-authored PRs are welcome and say so. The template's checklist is the review contract:

    • the change is scoped to one concern; unrelated cleanups are separate PRs
    • tests added or updated; pixi run pytest test -q is green (paste the summary line)
    • live smoke run for lifecycle / launcher / monitor changes (paste the command and the counters you read)
    • opencda/ edits are recorded in the patch ledger
    • docs updated on the owning page; mkdocs build --strict passes
    • no new algorithm-name dispatch; capabilities declared instead
    • no generated files (_runtime/, artifacts/, checkpoints, recordings), no secrets, hostnames, absolute paths or private URLs
    • the PR description states what an agent could not verify (no GPU, no CARLA) so a maintainer can

docs.title: Reporting
docs.text: Lead with the outcome. Failing tests are reported with their output, never summarised away; a skipped verification step is named as skipped. A number quoted anywhere (speed, reward, pass count) comes from a run you can point to.

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text: One sealed lifecycle, many replaceable joints. The framework fixes how a run executes — world, traffic, agents, observe, act, reward, learn, telemetry — and turns every part an experiment might vary into a plugin selected by configuration. The intended workflow: a research project varies one component behind one joint, and the validated component integrates back without the loop ever changing shape. This page is the map of those joints; Replace a Component is the practice — the mechanism, then one worked page per kind, of which Add an Algorithm covers the largest.

docs.title: The four zones
docs.text:
zone contents import rule opencda_marl/_kernel/ the complete lifecycle: scenario manager, traffic, agent manager, envs, policy manager, checkpointing never imports builtin — the kernel knows contracts, not implementations opencda_marl/api/ every contract and every register_* door the only surface plugins and external code touch opencda_marl/plugins/ the one plugin system: discovery, loading, freeze, rollback — opencda_marl/builtin/ the framework's own plugin set (learners, planners, agents, extractors, rewards, intent providers) registers through the same doors an external package would

The boundary is enforced, not conventional: test/basic/test_architecture.py parses the imports of every kernel module and fails on a violation.

docs.title: The run loop and its joints
docs.text:
flowchart TB SB[scenario config] --> SM[scenario manager] SM --> TM[traffic manager] TM --> AM[agent manager] AM --> OBS[observe] OBS --> ACT[act] ACT --> RWD[reward] RWD --> LRN[learn] LRN --> TEL["telemetry / monitor"] TEL --> AM P1([planner]) -.-> TM P2([population mix]) -.-> TM P3([agent type]) -.-> AM P4([intent provider]) -.-> AM P5([observation extractor]) -.-> OBS P6([algorithm]) -.-> ACT P7(["reward calculatorreward / objective /preference profiles"]) -.-> RWD P8([traffic view backend]) -.-> TEL

Solid arrows are the sealed loop; dashed nodes are the joints. The loop is identical on both backends — CARLA (marl/, pcma/, momarl/ families) and SUMO (sumo-marl/) — so a component validated on one transfers to the other unchanged. The one exception is the agent kind: an agent factory drives a CARLA vehicle, and on SUMO a population key is only a label (vehicles outside the learner's population drive under SUMO's own car-following model).

docs.title: Replaceable joints
docs.text:
Every joint is a kind in one unified registry. Registration happens at import time through opencda_marl.api; pixi run python -m opencda_marl.plugins lists what is registered and from where.

kind contract register through selected by built-ins algorithm Policy protocol (+IntentPolicy for path heads), PolicyCapabilities — opencda_marl.api.policy register_algorithm MARL.algorithm masac, pcmasac, mappo, pcmappo, matd3, pcmatd3, dqn, q_learning planner class with constructor (world, config) register_component("planner", key) scenario.traffic.planner.type marl agent factory (vehicle, carla_map, config); resolved on CARLA only register_component("agent", key) agents.agent_type (globally) or agents.population.mix (per vehicle) marl, rule_based, vanilla, behavior; the no-learner baselines are exactly behavior, vanilla and rule_based (BASELINE_AGENT_TYPES is closed) reward_calculator produces RewardOutput per agent (opencda_marl.api.contracts) register_component("reward_calculator", key) MARL.components.reward_calculator default observation_extractor maps raw observations to the declared feature vector register_component("observation_extractor", key) MARL.components.observation_extractor default intent_provider IntentProvider: spawn context → RouteIntentDecision (opencda_marl.api.intent) register_component("intent_provider", key) MARL.action_space.path.provider: <any registered key>; without it, MARL.action_space.path.selector names a built-in (keep_current→tao_fixed, random_legal→naive_random, rule_based→rule_based_path, learned→the policy bridge) tao_fixed, naive_random, rule_based_path reward_profile a named parameter table register_reward_profile MARL.reward_profile simple_progress_v1, dense_intersection_v1, cooperative_intersection_v1, competitive_intersection_v1/_v2 objective_profile the objective vector definition register_objective_profile MARL.objective_mode cooperative_pref_v1, competitive_ordering_v1 preference_profile a named preference table (by entry direction) register_preference_profile MARL.preference.profile balanced, asymmetric_split, reversed_asymmetric_split, mild_asymmetric_split context_encoder module with forward(sequences) / forward_padded(sequences, lengths) over the ego-first, nearest-first neighbour sequence; constructor (input_size, hidden_size, num_layers) register_component("context_encoder", key) MARL.<algo>.context_encoder lstm your own axis whatever your experiment needs register_component("your_kind", key) — unknown kinds are accepted and listed your config key —

How a plugin package reaches the registry — an opencda_marl.plugins entry point, MARL.plugins in config, $OPENCDA_MARL_PLUGINS, or a module dropped into builtin/algorithms/contrib/ — is covered in Add an Algorithm.

docs.title: Ports
docs.text:
Not everything replaceable is a registry kind; these are seams by contract rather than by key:

port contract where drive the scenarios from your own RL loop PettingZoo-style ParallelEnv opencda_marl/envs/parallel_env.py a new monitor chart vanilla JS against the /api/runs/... endpoints, no build step opencda_marl/telemetry/static/ feed the live traffic view from a new backend collect_traffic_view() / collect_traffic_geometry() on the env opencda_marl/telemetry/traffic_view.py documents the file shapes, including the y_up frame flag a new scenario or profile a YAML stating only what changes opencda_marl/_bundled/configs/<family>/<scenario>/, or the same path under your own --marl-config-root a new deterministic traffic recording record mode writes one as run output; adopting it as a benchmark is a copy into the package artifacts/recordings/ → opencda_marl/_bundled/recordings/

docs.title: Adjustable seams
docs.text:
The joints above swap implementations; these config-level seams change what the fixed loop does — each one is a configuration axis:

seam key meaning mixed autonomy agents.population: {mix: {marl: 0.5, rule_based: 0.5}, seed: N} shares exact over each window of resolution vehicles, reproducible per seed (a shorter prefix only approximates them; live flows draw flow by flow). The learner commands (speed and path actions, at spawn and at the approach decision zone) and learns from its own population, agents.agent_type, only; background vehicles keep their demand routes and stay in the traffic context. The mix must name agents.agent_type, or the learner gets no vehicle. On CARLA the mix is checked at construction: a mix without the learning population is rejected, a zero learner share warns, and every positive-share name must be a registered agent type (matched exactly, case-sensitive). On SUMO every other name is background traffic SUMO drives itself what one path action means MARL.action_space.path.provider: <registered intent_provider> the built-in semantic action (left / straight / right / keep) is the example; a provider declares its own alternatives, mask and head width through opencda_marl.api.path_action when the path decision happens MARL.action_space.path.decision_zone: {trigger: spawn \| approach, distance_m} decide at spawn, or on approaching the junction committed exit lanes in the observation MARL.<algo>.features.committed_exit_lanes: <width> per exit lane, how many other vehicles at the same junction have already committed to it, in <width> slots; off by default, and the state dimension changes with it per-vehicle objective preferences agents.preference: {mode, sampler, dim, alpha, seed, regime} the spawn-time sampler; regime: aligned \| conflicting decides whether preference-heterogeneous vehicles meet traffic determinism scenario.traffic.mode: replay \| live \| record the bundled recordings are evaluation ground truth per-vehicle driver behaviour metadata.driver on a spawn event reaches the agent factory as config["spawn_metadata"], and on SUMO is applied to background vehicles (speed_factor, tau, min_gap, imperfection, accel, decel) the SUMO frame convention runtime.coordinate_landmarks junction landmarks in CARLA's frame decide y_flip; a <net>_landmarks.json (or <net>_junction_graph.json) next to the network is found without configuration, keyed by junction id either flat, {"12": [x, y]}, or nested, {"junctions": {"12": {"centre": [x, y]}}}. A map with none keeps the default, no y flip, so a CARLA town export needs landmarks the map, on both backends CARLA: scenario.map.town or scenario.map.xodr_path; SUMO: runtime.sumo_cfg an .xodr builds the CARLA world from the road network alone. SUMO does not read scenario.map: it loads the network named by the <net-file> of the .sumocfg at runtime.sumo_cfg, so a .sumocfg naming the derived .net.xml pairs the two, and SUMO reads that network in CARLA's frame only with the landmarks above. No .sumocfg names the derived town networks in opencda_marl/assets/maps/, and no landmarks ship for any town (Run Experiments)

Historical note: the path-intent axis is identified as route_intent in code, metadata and traces — the name predates the pluggable path action. It still covers what the axis does (choose the way out of the junction, by whatever alternatives its provider offers); the preference sampler, which conditions objectives rather than routes, moved to agents.preference (agents.route_intent.preference still works).

docs.title: Rules the joints live under
docs.text:
• Load once, then freeze. Plugins register at import time during startup; afterwards the registry is frozen — no hot reload, so what ran is what was listed.
  • No silent shadowing. Overriding an existing key — built-ins included — requires override=True; a typo cannot replace a component quietly.
  • Version rollback. A plugin whose declared API version mismatches is rolled back as a unit, across every kind it registered.
  • Config composes. Three layers per scenario reference (default.yaml → base.yaml → profile), include: for reuse, external roots via --marl-config-root; a profile states only what it changes.
  • Contracts are pinned by tests, not by convention: test/basic/test_architecture.py (zones), test/route_intent/ (registry, policy contract, components, intent), test/basic/test_config_lint.py (every shipped profile resolves).

docs.title: An Agent Type
docs.text:
An agent type is the driver behind one vehicle: the factory is called per spawned vehicle and returns whatever drives it — a learner's actuator, a rule-based baseline, a scripted human model. The built-ins (marl, rule_based, vanilla, behavior) register through the same door yours does.

Kind agent, factory (vehicle, carla_map, config), selected by agents.agent_type — or per vehicle through the population mix, which is where this kind earns its keep. (Mechanics on Replace a Component.)

CARLA only

The agent kind is resolved on the CARLA backend, one agent per spawned vehicle. On SUMO a population key is a label: vehicles outside the learner's population drive under SUMO's own car-following model, and a registered agent factory never runs. The no-learner baselines are exactly behavior, vanilla and rule_based; a registered agent type is never treated as one.

docs.title: Worked example
docs.text:
The built-in factories compose, so a new type can be a re-parameterisation of an existing one — here, the behavior baseline slowed down, reading its own config section:

from opencda_marl.api import register_component
from opencda_marl.builtin.agents.agent_factory import build_behavior_agent


@register_component("agent", "cautious_driver")
def build_cautious_driver(vehicle, carla_map, config):
    """The behavior baseline, slowed down; reads agents.cautious_driver."""
    cfg = dict(config or {})
    cfg["behavior"] = {**(cfg.get("behavior") or {}),
                       "max_speed": 35,
                       **(cfg.get("cautious_driver") or {})}
    return build_behavior_agent(vehicle, carla_map, cfg)

Selected globally, or as a share of the population — a mixed-autonomy experiment is just a distribution over registered agent types, with shares exact over every window of resolution (default 100) vehicles and reproducible per seed:

agents:
  agent_type: cautious_driver          # everyone
  # or:
  population:
    mix: {marl: 0.7, cautious_driver: 0.3}
    seed: 7

The learner commands — and learns from — its own population only, so the mixed run stays a clean experiment. On CARLA the mix is checked at construction: it must name the learning population (agents.agent_type), and every name with a positive share must be a registered agent type (matched exactly, case-sensitive), so a typo fails before the first episode rather than at its first spawn.

docs.title: Verify
docs.text:
On a CARLA profile: copy momarl/intersection/speed_only_pcmappo.yaml to my_configs/momarl/intersection/cautious_mix.yaml, add agents.population: {mix: {marl: 0.7, cautious_driver: 0.3}, seed: 7} and MARL.plugins: [<your module>], start a CARLA server, and run it:

pixi run python opencda.py -t momarl/intersection/cautious_mix --marl --marl-config-root my_configs

Then read the spawn log or the trace: each vehicle's agent type is in its spawn metadata, and the shares hold exactly over every 100 consecutive draws of the population pattern.

docs.title: Add an Algorithm
docs.text:
The framework owns the pipeline — observation extraction, reward shaping, route legality masks, episode lifecycle, checkpointing, metrics. An algorithm owns only the decision. This page shows how to plug one in.

You never edit a file under opencda_marl/ to add an algorithm. If you find yourself doing so, that is a bug in the seam — please report it.

docs.title: Two integration levels
docs.text:
Level Who owns the training loop Use when Environment port — OpenCDAMARLParallelEnv You You want to drive the benchmark with any RL code (SB3, RLlib, CleanRL, your own loop) against a standard obs-in / speed-out interface Policy port — Policy + register_algorithm The framework You want the framework's training infrastructure: matrix launcher, checkpoints, the metrics store and monitor, route-intent heads

The built-in PCMA algorithms are level-2 citizens; both levels see identical observations, rewards, and execution, which is what keeps results comparable.

docs.title: Level 1: the ParallelEnv port
docs.text:
A PettingZoo-style parallel environment: observations out, target speeds in, framework-computed rewards back — with the per-component breakdown, objective vectors, and preference vectors in infos so you can re-shape rewards in your own loop without forking the pipeline.

The engine installs as a library — the wheel bundles the sumo-marl config family, the lite traffic replay and the intersection SUMO network, so this runs without a repository checkout; torch is installed as a dependency but this path never imports it:

pixi run wheel                           # builds dist/opencda_marl-*.whl (no PyPI release yet)
pip install dist/opencda_marl-*.whl      # SUMO runs out of the box

from opencda_marl.envs.parallel_env import OpenCDAMARLParallelEnv

env = OpenCDAMARLParallelEnv.from_scenario(
    "sumo-marl/intersection/route_speed_only_pcmappo",
    overrides={"MARL": {"external": {"features": {
        "rel_x": 1, "rel_y": 1, "heading_angle": 1, "dist_to_intersection": 1}}}})
observations, infos = env.reset()
while not env.episode_over:          # env.agents is empty before the first spawn
    actions = {agent: my_policy(observations[agent]) for agent in env.agents}
    observations, rewards, terminations, truncations, infos = env.step(actions)
env.close()

Contract notes:

  • Actions are target speeds in km/h (the planner and controller stay fixed — that is the matched protocol that makes comparisons fair). An agent you stop sending actions for is handed back to SUMO's own car-following model (under the scenario's world.sumo_rl_runtime_mode); an agent you have not commanded yet keeps the departure speed it spawned with. To control every agent, send an action for every agent in env.agents.
  • Loop on env.episode_over, not on env.agents: vehicles spawn over time, so the live set is empty at the start of a replay and between waves of traffic.
  • Agents join and leave mid-episode as vehicles spawn and terminate; a terminating agent appears one final time in the step returns (infos[agent]["event"] is success / collision / removed).
  • The scenario declares the observation vector (MARL.external.features, in the profile or through overrides as above) — the benchmark defines the observation space, not the algorithm. The observation width follows those features (plus the preference entries when the scenario conditions on preferences), not the profile's MARL.state_dim, which belongs to the profile's own learner. The reference resolves exactly as on the command line (a configs/ root under the working directory, OPENCDA_MARL_CONFIG_ROOTS, then the bundled configs), and a profile's include: list is composed.
  • Path intent stays framework-side for this port (the port's actions are speeds): MARL.action_space.path.selector picks rule-based / random-legal / keep-current / a learned head, and MARL.action_space.path.provider names a registered path action of your own (Architecture has the seam map). Path actions are not exposed over the external port yet.
  • pettingzoo / gymnasium are soft dependencies (installed in the pixi environment; the wheel's [ports] extra adds them): without them the same API works by duck typing and observation_space() raises an actionable error; with them the class is a genuine pettingzoo.ParallelEnv with real Gymnasium spaces.
  • from_scenario supports the SUMO backend today; CARLA lands with the parallel-training work.

docs.title: Level 2: the Policy port
docs.text: The rest of this page covers level 2.

docs.title: The contract
docs.text:
Two protocols in opencda_marl/api/policy.py:

  • Policy — the speed controller. Required.
  • IntentPolicy — optional one-shot route-intent capability, needed only for action_space.mode: path_speed with a learned route selector.

A Policy implements seven methods and exposes two attributes:

Member Meaning select_action(multi_agent_obs, ego_agent_id, training) Target speed in km/h for one agent, or None (warmup) to leave the vehicle to the backend's own driver for that step: the vanilla driver on CARLA, SUMO's car-following model on SUMO (a vehicle never commanded keeps its departure speed) store_transition(obs, ego_id, action, reward, next_obs, done) Record one transition update() One learning step; returns a metrics dict reset_episode() Clear per-episode state get_training_info() Diagnostics for the monitor and metric sinks save(path) / load(path) Checkpoint round-trip max_action Upper speed clamp, km/h supports_batched_actions True to receive one batched select_actions call per step instead of N per-agent calls

Observations arrive as {agent_id: state_vector} — every live agent, so a centralized critic can see the whole scene. The ego agent's own vector is multi_agent_obs[ego_agent_id].

docs.title: A minimal algorithm
docs.text:
# my_project/constant_policy.py
from opencda_marl.api import register_algorithm


class ConstantSpeedPolicy:
    supports_batched_actions = False

    def __init__(self, config, state_dim, action_dim):
        self.max_action = float(config.get("max_action", 45.0))
        self.speed = float(config.get("constant_speed", 25.0))

    def select_action(self, multi_agent_obs, ego_agent_id, training=True):
        return self.speed

    def store_transition(self, multi_agent_obs, ego_agent_id, action, reward,
                         next_multi_agent_obs, done):
        pass

    def update(self):
        return {}

    def reset_episode(self):
        pass

    def get_training_info(self):
        return {"algorithm_type": "constant"}

    def save(self, filepath):
        pass

    def load(self, filepath):
        pass


@register_algorithm("constant", label="Constant")
def build_constant(config, *, state_dim, action_dim):
    return ConstantSpeedPolicy(config, state_dim, action_dim)

docs.title: Making it discoverable
docs.text:
The registration runs when the module is imported. Four ways to get it imported -- none of them touch opencda_marl/:

route when to use your own package with an entry point a research repository that pip installs the framework — the standard workflow drop the module into opencda_marl/builtin/algorithms/contrib/ you cloned this repository; contrib modules are auto-imported, zero configuration MARL.plugins: [my_project.constant_policy] in the scenario YAML pin the plugin to the experiment; loaded at initialize for every run, before either backend resolves a component, so it works with the matrix launcher, the monitor and evaluation OPENCDA_MARL_PLUGINS=my_project.constant_policy (or a .py path; os.pathsep-separated) ad-hoc, no config edit 
[project.entry-points."opencda_marl.plugins"]
constant = "my_project.constant_policy"

Declare the contract version your package targets as a module attribute — OPENCDA_MARL_POLICY_API = 1 — next to your registrations. The engine (opencda_marl.plugins.POLICY_API_VERSION) rolls back and reports a plugin built against a different contract version instead of letting it misbehave at run time; omitting the attribute skips the check.

The built-in learners are themselves a plugin (opencda_marl/builtin/algorithms/, loaded through the entry point the wheel declares on itself), so a plugin is a peer, not a special case — the engine imports no learners at all. python -m opencda_marl.plugins lists everything that is registered and where it came from; a plugin that fails to import is reported there and in the error you get when its name is requested.

Your package can ship its own scenario profile under its own config root and inherit the framework's family default and scenario base:

pixi run python opencda.py -t sumo-marl/intersection/my_profile --marl \
    --marl-config-root path/to/my_project/configs

The smallest complete learner -- one file, one profile -- is opencda_marl/builtin/algorithms/contrib/random_speed.py with opencda_marl/_bundled/configs/sumo-marl/intersection/random_speed.yaml; run it with pixi run python opencda.py -t sumo-marl/intersection/random_speed --marl.

docs.title: What the framework does for a plain policy
docs.text: A policy that does not subclass BaseAlgorithm still gets: checkpoints (save/load are called with the per-episode / best / latest paths), world reloads on CARLA (the snapshot reads only what the policy has), and a metrics store for the monitor -- the manager records every update() result (every outputs.metrics_store.log_frequency calls) and every episode summary under metrics/<algorithm>/<run>/, where <algorithm> is the key you registered (a BaseAlgorithm subclass's store lands there too).

docs.title: What a checkpoint should hold
docs.text: A checkpoint should not carry the run's configuration. The config your factory receives is your MARL.<section> block plus training_mode (and reward_dim when vector_rewards injects it) and the tensorboard and metrics_store blocks the manager merges in from outputs.* (directories under outputs.root_dir, the run name). Its top-level values arrive resolved, but its list and dict values are OmegaConf nodes, each of which keeps a reference to the whole run config: pickled as they are, they ship every section. The built-in learners store self.checkpoint_config(), which every BaseAlgorithm inherits from TrainingLogger, instead of self.config. It is a plain copy without those two blocks, with any value that is an absolute filesystem path replaced by <absolute path removed>; every hyperparameter is kept. Interpolations inside nested blocks are kept as written. A top-level value that resolved to an absolute path is replaced, but a path inside a longer string (run@${outputs.root_dir}) is saved as it resolved, so keep such strings out of your section's top level. A BaseAlgorithm subclass that writes its config in its own save should store the same. Any list or dict it reads from its config and saves separately should go in as portable_config(...) from opencda_marl.builtin.algorithms.training_logger, the function behind checkpoint_config(). It takes an OmegaConf node or a plain dict or list, returns plain dicts and lists, and replaces absolute paths the same way. OmegaConf.to_container(...) raises on a plain dict, for example in a learner built from plain dicts, and keeps absolute paths. A list of plain numbers can also go in as list(...). A policy that does not subclass BaseAlgorithm can store portable_config(config), which also leaves those two blocks out.

docs.title: Configuring it
docs.text:
The shared extractor's position_x and position_y features are absolute map coordinates in the common CARLA frame. They read the explicit normalized position fields; location is a fallback because legacy CARLA observations use that dictionary for junction-relative coordinates. Use rel_x and rel_y for the relative position. The SUMO position features have always read this way.

For replay vehicles with assigned junction geometry, rel_x/rel_y are the vehicle's map position minus that junction's center. dist_to_intersection and the approach decision-zone radius use the planar distance to the same center on both backends. This replaces CARLA's former nearest-waypoint vector and entry-distance trigger. Legacy planners without junction geometry retain their adapter-provided distances; the legacy location alias is unchanged.

The config section is the algorithm name by default. Features declared here drive the shared observation extractor — this is how your algorithm gets a state vector without writing any extraction code:

MARL:
  algorithm: constant
  state_dim: 3
  action_space:
    mode: speed_only
  constant:
    constant_speed: 27.5
    max_action: 45.0
    features:
      rel_x: 1
      rel_y: 1
      speed: 1

state_dim must equal the summed feature widths plus the preference dimension when preference conditioning is on. A mismatch is logged as a warning at construction — the configured value still wins, because it is baked into saved checkpoints.

docs.title: Declaring capabilities
docs.text:
register_algorithm accepts:

Argument Default Effect label uppercased key Display name in tables, logs and the monitor config_section the key Which MARL.<section> block reaches your factory multi_agent True False routes single-agent observations instead: select_action(state, training) and store_transition(state, action, reward, next_state, done) on the agent's own state reward_aggregation "per_agent" "team_mean" gives every agent the team-mean reward supports_intent False True declares the IntentPolicy capability vector_rewards False True injects reward_dim for objective-vector runs override False Required to replace an existing registration

The framework dispatches on these declarations. There is no isinstance check and no name list to join.

A single-agent policy (multi_agent=False) returns the target speed from select_action too, unless its class declares returns_action_index = True: then select_action returns an index into the policy's speed_actions list, the framework drives that list entry, and the index is what store_transition receives back as action. The declaration is read, never inferred — owning a speed_actions table does not make a policy index-returning (the bundled DQN returns speeds; tabular Q-learning returns indices).

docs.title: Adding route-intent support
docs.text:
To support learned route selection, implement IntentPolicy — or inherit the standard implementation from RouteHeadMixin, which is what the built-in families do:

from opencda_marl.builtin.algorithms.route_head import RouteHeadMixin


class MyIntentPolicy(RouteHeadMixin, ConstantSpeedPolicy):
    route_head_cls = "HybridRouteSACHead"   # or HybridRoutePPOHead
    route_head_shares_optimizer = False     # True for PPO-family heads


@register_algorithm("my_intent", supports_intent=True)
def build(config, *, state_dim, action_dim):
    return MyIntentPolicy(config, state_dim, action_dim)

The mixin requires self.device (and self.optimizer when route_head_shares_optimizer = True).

Route intent is one-shot: the policy chooses once per vehicle at spawn from the legal set the framework supplies, and the reward arrives at that vehicle's terminal event — hence store_pending / finalize_terminal rather than a per-step transition. Illegal actions are masked before sampling; never select a masked-out index.

Registering with supports_intent=True without implementing the methods fails at manager construction with a message naming what is missing, rather than misbehaving at run time.

docs.title: Beyond algorithms: components and profiles
docs.text: Research rarely stops at the learner. The same plugin door (entry point, MARL.plugins, OPENCDA_MARL_PLUGINS, contrib/) carries every other registration your package makes at import time — planners, agent types, intent providers, observation extractors, reward calculators, the profile tables, and axes of your own. Replace a Component is the mechanism, with one worked page per kind; overriding an existing key — built-ins included — always requires override=True, so a typo cannot shadow one silently. The per-vehicle local planner still lives inside the vendored OpenCDA behavior stack and is not yet an axis.

docs.title: Verifying your algorithm
docs.text:
pixi run pytest test/route_intent/test_policy_registry.py -q

That file registers a policy defined entirely inside the test and drives it through MARLManager — copy its shape to smoke-test your own before launching a training run.

docs.title: Known rough edges
docs.text:
Honest notes, so you do not discover these the hard way:

  • Actions are km/h, not a normalized action space. Conversion belongs in an env-side action space; until that lands it is part of the contract.
  • None doubles as the "leave this vehicle to the backend's own driver" signal during warmup.
  • Preference vectors are appended to the end of the state vector; policies that need them slice the last pref_dim entries.

docs.title: An Intent Provider
docs.text:
An intent provider decides, per vehicle, which way it goes at the junction. The same callable serves both decision timings: at spawn (default), or at the junction approach when the decision zone is configured (MARL.action_space.path.decision_zone: {trigger: approach, distance_m: 30}).

Kind intent_provider, factory (intent_cfg, planner, *, marl_manager, training, previous) returning a callable spawn context → RouteIntentDecision | None. (Mechanics on Replace a Component.)

docs.title: Worked example
docs.text:
The public helpers in opencda_marl.api.route_intent do the heavy lifting — legal candidates from the planner's route table, the feasibility mask, and the decision record the rest of the lifecycle consumes:

from opencda_marl.api import register_component
from opencda_marl.api.route_intent import (
    RouteIntent, build_candidates_with_diagnostics, build_decision,
    build_mask, resolve_route)


@register_component("intent_provider", "prefer_right")
def build_prefer_right(intent_cfg, planner, *, marl_manager=None,
                       training=True, previous=None):
    """Turn right whenever the junction allows it; otherwise keep."""
    def provider(context):
        event = context["event"]
        meta = event.metadata or {}
        if meta.get("entry_direction") is None:
            return None
        candidates, diagnostics = build_candidates_with_diagnostics(
            planner=planner,
            junction_id=int(event.junction_id),
            entry_direction=str(meta["entry_direction"]),
            entry_lane_idx=int(meta.get("entry_lane_idx", meta.get("lane_id", -1))),
            original_route_id=int(event.route_id),
        )
        if not candidates:
            return None
        mask = build_mask(candidates)
        intent = (RouteIntent.RIGHT if mask.get(RouteIntent.RIGHT)
                  else RouteIntent.KEEP)
        candidate = resolve_route(intent, candidates, mask,
                                  original_route_id=int(event.route_id))
        return build_decision(requested_intent=intent, candidate=candidate,
                              mask=mask,
                              original_route_id=int(event.route_id),
                              diagnostics=diagnostics)
    return provider

Selection runs through the action space: MARL.action_space.path.provider names any registered intent_provider, next to the built-ins:

MARL:
  action_space:
    mode: path_speed
    path:
      selector: rule_based     # a built-in selector: no learned head
      provider: prefer_right

Named next to a built-in selector (rule_based, random_legal, keep_current), the provider decides alone and no learned head is built. With selector: learned, or with provider named alone, it drives the learned-head lifecycle and owns the head.

The previous argument is the provider being replaced on a world reload; state that should outlive the rebuild (the built-in random provider carries its RNG this way) is handed over through it.

docs.title: Verify
docs.text:
Copy sumo-marl/intersection/route_rule_path_pcmappo.yaml to my_configs/sumo-marl/intersection/prefer_right.yaml, add MARL.action_space.path.provider: prefer_right and MARL.plugins: [<the module holding build_prefer_right>], run it, and read the decision counters — every spawn carries a route_intent decision record in its metadata, and the monitor's episode summaries count them:

pixi run python opencda.py -t sumo-marl/intersection/prefer_right --marl --marl-config-root my_configs

docs.title: An Observation Extractor
docs.text:
The extractor is what the learner sees: every step it turns the raw per-agent observation dicts into the state vectors the policy consumes. The policy manager constructs one per run; the declared feature set (MARL.<algo>.features) decides the vector layout, and the extractor decides how raw values become features.

Kind observation_extractor, constructor (config, algorithm_name, *, multi_agent), one method that matters: extract(observations) → {agent: np.ndarray}. Selected by MARL.components.observation_extractor. (Mechanics on Replace a Component.)

docs.title: Worked example
docs.text:
Subclass the default and transform its output — a robustness check in six lines:

import numpy as np

from opencda_marl.api import register_component
from opencda_marl.builtin.extractors import ObservationExtractor


@register_component("observation_extractor", "clipped")
class ClippedExtractor(ObservationExtractor):
    """Clips every normalised feature, as a saturated sensor would."""

    def extract(self, observations):
        states = super().extract(observations)
        return {agent: np.clip(vec, -5.0, 5.0) for agent, vec in states.items()}

MARL:
  components:
    observation_extractor: clipped

docs.title: The one contract to respect
docs.text: The state dimension is part of the learner's contract: transform features freely, but change the width only together with the learner — or declare the feature set differently via MARL.<algo>.features, which the default extractor already handles (that is also how the committed_exit_lanes channel is switched on and sized).

docs.title: Verify
docs.text:
A width mismatch fails loudly at network construction; a value bug does not. Run a short scenario and compare a logged state vector against the raw observation it came from before trusting a training curve:

pixi run python opencda.py -t sumo-marl/intersection/route_speed_only_pcmappo --marl

docs.title: A Planner
docs.text:
The planner owns the route table: it finds the junctions, groups their entry lanes, and generates the candidate routes traffic can drive. The traffic manager constructs it once per scenario and queries it for every spawn — on both backends — so replacing it changes what demand is.

Kind planner, constructor (world, config), selected by scenario.traffic.planner.type. (Mechanics — discovery, freeze, override, validate — on Replace a Component.)

docs.title: Worked example
docs.text:
The built-in marl planner exposes its route queries as methods, so the practical route is subclassing it and changing exactly the behaviour you want to vary:

from opencda_marl.api import register_component
from opencda_marl.builtin.planners.marl_planner import MARLPlanner


@register_component("planner", "keep_right")
class KeepRightPlanner(MARLPlanner):
    """Demand routes prefer a right turn wherever the junction has one."""

    def get_random_route(self, junction_id, visualize=False):
        right = self.get_random_route_by_type(junction_id, "right", visualize)
        return right if right is not None else super().get_random_route(
            junction_id, visualize)

scenario:
  traffic:
    planner:
      type: keep_right

A from-scratch planner implements the same query surface the built-in has (get_junctions, get_routes, get_random_route*); start from opencda_marl/builtin/planners/marl_planner.py as the reference.

docs.title: Verify
docs.text:
Run the SUMO smoke and watch the Traffic view in the monitor — the routes actually driven are the planner's output:

pixi run python opencda.py -t sumo-marl/intersection/route_rule_path_pcmappo --marl

docs.title: Profile Tables
docs.text:
Rewards, objectives and preferences are data, not code: named tables selected by key. An experiment that only changes numbers — a reward weight, an objective split, a preference assignment — ships a profile, keeps every line of framework code identical, and stays diffable as configuration.

Kinds reward_profile, objective_profile, preference_profile; registered by register_reward_profile / register_objective_profile / register_preference_profile; selected by MARL.reward_profile, MARL.objective_mode, MARL.preference.profile. (Mechanics on Replace a Component.)

docs.title: Worked example
docs.text:
from opencda_marl.api import register_reward_profile

register_reward_profile("lab_rewards", {"rewards": {"success": 500.0}})

MARL:
  reward_profile: lab_rewards

register_objective_profile and register_preference_profile work the same way. The built-in tables are the reference shapes to copy from — they live next to their register functions in opencda_marl/api/rewards.py, objectives.py and preferences.py (e.g. competitive_intersection_v2, cooperative_pref_v1, balanced).

docs.title: How the three relate
docs.text:
• A reward profile parameterises the calculator's terms.
  • An objective profile defines the objective vector those terms are folded into.
  • A preference profile assigns the weights over that vector — by entry direction here; the per-vehicle sampler is configuration instead (agents.preference), because sampled preferences are a distribution, not a table.

The PCMA learners are built on exactly this split.

docs.title: Verify
docs.text: A typo'd key fails at initialize (unknown profiles do not resolve), and overriding an existing name requires override=True. The record that makes a summary attributable to its numbers is the run's own config: the selecting keys live in the profile YAML that launched it, and matrix cells persist their fully merged runtime profile next to the run.

docs.title: A Reward Calculator
docs.text:
The calculator is the structure of the reward — which terms exist and how they are computed. Changing the numbers is a reward profile; a new calculator is for new terms or new shaping. Each env constructs one at initialize and calls it every step.

Kind reward_calculator, constructor (reward_params, reward_spec), selected by MARL.components.reward_calculator. (Mechanics on Replace a Component.)

docs.title: Worked example
docs.text:
The built-in exposes its terms as methods, and the term methods are shared by both backends' entry points (calculate_carla / calculate_sumo) — so one term can be reshaped in isolation and the change holds on CARLA and SUMO alike:

from opencda_marl.api import register_component
from opencda_marl.builtin.rewards.calculator import RewardCalculator


@register_component("reward_calculator", "impatient")
class ImpatientRewards(RewardCalculator):
    """Doubles the progress signal; every other term inherited."""

    def calculate_progress_reward(self, current_observation, previous_observation):
        return 2.0 * super().calculate_progress_reward(
            current_observation, previous_observation)

MARL:
  components:
    reward_calculator: impatient

For multi-objective work the calculator's output feeds the objective vector defined by MARL.objective_mode (Profile Tables); the reward/objective split means a new term composes with preference conditioning instead of fighting it.

docs.title: Verify
docs.text:
Reward changes are the easiest to fool yourself with: read the per-term components the calculator emits (RewardOutput.components), not just the total, and compare one episode against the unmodified calculator before training on it:

pixi run python opencda.py -t sumo-marl/intersection/route_speed_only_pcmappo --marl

docs.title: PCMA: Preference-Coordinated Learners
docs.text:
The preference-conditioned learners in OpenCDA-MARL — PCMASAC, PCMAPPO and the conditioning-only PCMATD3 — build on Preference Coordinated Multi-agent Policy Optimization (PCMA):

Pengxin Wang, Lihao Guo, Yi Xie, Bo Liu, Siyang Cao, Jingdi Chen. Learning Coordinated Preference for Multi-Objective Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning. arXiv:2606.14693, 2026. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.14693

The paper's setting is cooperative multi-objective MARL: a team optimises several, possibly conflicting objectives, and the conflicts run across agents as well as across objectives. PCMA gives every agent its own preference over the objectives and lets the agents coordinate those preferences — shifting them so that the team's trade-offs are complementary rather than identical. The signal-free intersection in this framework is the paper's traffic-control scenario.

These learners are the framework's variant, not a reproduction of the paper's algorithm: preferences are assigned (layer 2 below) and shifted by a deterministic head, with a vector critic and a separation term, and the paper's Dirichlet preference planner is not implemented. Do not report a result from them as a result for the paper's PCMA. This page states exactly what the implementation does, so results can be reproduced and the learners extended.

docs.title: Three layers
docs.text: A PCMA run is configured in three places, each independent of the others.

docs.title: 1. Objectives — MARL.objective_mode
docs.text:
The reward pipeline computes per-agent reward components (progress, success, step penalty, collision, …; MARL.reward_profile selects their weights). An objective profile groups components into \(K\) objectives and the environment emits a vector \(\mathbf r_i \in \mathbb R^K\) per agent per step alongside the scalar reward:

objective_mode objectives components cooperative_pref_v1 efficiency, safety progress + success + step_penalty; collision competitive_ordering_v1 efficiency, interaction_risk progress + success + step_penalty; collision

MARL.reward_mode decides what the learner is trained on: objective_vector hands \(\mathbf r_i\) to a learner that declares vector_rewards and runs a vector critic; otherwise the learner receives the scalarised \(\mathbf w_i^\top \mathbf r_i\). Profiles are defined in opencda_marl/api/objectives.py.

docs.title: 2. Preferences — who holds which weight vector
docs.text:
Each agent \(i\) carries a raw preference \(\mathbf w_i\) on the simplex (\(K = 2\) today). It is assigned once per vehicle, in this order:

  1. Per-vehicle at spawn (agents.preference, used by the momarl/ and sumo-marl/ experiment profiles): the traffic manager samples a preference for every spawned vehicle. regime: aligned gives everyone \([0.5, 0.5]\); regime: conflicting alternates \([0.75, 0.25]\) / \([0.25, 0.75]\) by spawn parity, so safety- and efficiency-weighted vehicles meet at the intersection.
  2. By profile (MARL.preference, used by the pcma/ profiles): a named table assigned by entry direction — balanced (\([0.5,0.5]\)), mild_asymmetric_split (\([0.6,0.4]\) for north/east, \([0.4,0.6]\) for south/west), asymmetric_split (0.8/0.2) and reversed_asymmetric_split.

injection: state_augmentation appends \(\mathbf w_i\) to the agent's state vector; MARL.state_dim therefore includes preference.dim. Every learner sees the preference in its observation — that alone is direct conditioning, and it is all PCMATD3 does.

docs.title: 3. Learners — MARL.pcmasac / MARL.pcmappo
docs.text:
Both learners share one preference mechanism, the shift head below on assigned preferences; they differ in the base algorithm (SAC off-policy with twin critics; PPO on-policy with GAE).

Preference shift. In internalpref modes the actor carries a shift head \(h\) on top of its observation features \(\phi_i = \phi(o_i, c_i)\) (\(c_i\) is the LSTM-encoded neighbour context):

\[ \boldsymbol\delta_i = \operatorname{clip}\big(\tanh h(\phi_i),\ \pm\beta\big),\qquad \tilde{\mathbf w}_i = \operatorname{norm}(\mathbf w_i + \boldsymbol\delta_i),\qquad \bar{\mathbf w}_i = \operatorname{norm}\big((1-m)\,\mathbf w_i + m\,\tilde{\mathbf w}_i\big) \]

with clip \(\beta\) (pref_shift_clip / pref_shift_max_abs), mix \(m\) (pref_shift_mix) and norm the projection back onto the simplex. The effective preference \(\bar{\mathbf w}_i\) — not the raw one — is what conditions the actor (pref_encoder_fusion, concat or film in PCMAPPO; an encoder-fusion head in PCMASAC). The head is initialised at zero shift, so training starts from plain direct conditioning.

Vector critic. With critic_mode: vector the critic outputs \(\mathbf Q(s,a) \in \mathbb R^K\) (PCMASAC) or a per-objective value head next to the scalar one (PCMAPPO, trained on per-objective returns with weight critic_vector_l2_coef). PCMASAC's actor then maximises the preference-scalarised value

\[ J_i = \mathbb E\big[\ \bar{\mathbf w}_i^\top \mathbf Q(s, a) - \alpha \log \pi(a \mid s)\ \big], \]

where pref_update_mode selects the weights: shifted_pref_actor (\(\bar{\mathbf w}_i\), gradients flow into the shift head — the shift-aware update), shifted_pref_actor_detached (same weights, no gradient), or direct_pref_actor (\(\mathbf w_i\)). PCMAPPO's policy gradient uses the advantage of the raw-preference scalarised reward \(\mathbf w_i^\top \mathbf r_i\); the shift acts through the actor's conditioning and the regularisers below.

Regularisers. Two terms added to the actor loss:

  • shift magnitude, pref_shift_l2_coef \(\cdot\ \|\boldsymbol\delta_i\|^2\), keeps the learned preference near the assigned one;
  • preference separation (pref_mode: internalpref_sep), a hinge on the effective preferences of agents in different raw-preference groups, pref_sep_coef \(\cdot \sum_{i<j,\ g_i \ne g_j} \max(0,\ \text{margin} - \|\bar{\mathbf w}_i - \bar{\mathbf w}_j\|)\), which keeps the shifted preferences of the two groups from collapsing onto each other. pref_sep_use_effective_pref: false applies it to \(\tilde{\mathbf w}_i\) instead.

The preference-conditioned learners also use reward_aggregation: team_mean (declared in their registration), so every agent is trained on the team's mean reward — the cooperative objective of the paper's setting.

docs.title: What to watch
docs.text:
In the monitor, beyond the usual losses:

  • SAC/pref_shift_l2, SAC/pref_shift_norm, SAC/pref_shift_abs_max (PCMASAC) and Pref/shift_l2 (PCMAPPO): how far the learned preferences moved. Zero throughout under internalpref or internalpref_sep means the shift head never trained. The SAC/pref_shift_* tags are logged only under those two modes, so if they are missing, pref_mode is direct (or the learner is plain MASAC).
  • SAC/effective_pref_obj_0_mean vs SAC/raw_pref_obj_0_mean (vector critic, internal modes): the direction of the shift.
  • SAC/pref_sep_loss, SAC/pref_sep_active_pairs (PCMASAC, logged only under internalpref_sep) / Pref/sep_loss (PCMAPPO): the separation term and how many cross-group pairs were in the batch.
  • Q_values/Q1_obj_k_mean (PCMASAC, vector critic) and Loss/vector_value (PCMAPPO): per-objective value estimates.

Each episode's competition summary (in the metrics archive and the evaluation output) splits success, collision and timeout rates and the average completion rank by preference group, so the two groups can be compared directly.

docs.title: Replace a Component
docs.text:
Every joint in the lifecycle swaps the same way. This page is the mechanism; each kind then has its own page with a complete worked example:

kind what it decides page algorithm how agents learn and act Add an Algorithm planner the route table the traffic drives A Planner agent the driver behind one vehicle An Agent Type intent_provider which way a vehicle goes at the junction An Intent Provider observation_extractor what the learner sees An Observation Extractor reward_calculator the structure of the reward A Reward Calculator reward_profile / objective_profile / preference_profile the numbers, as named tables Profile Tables

The full map — every joint's contract, door, config key and built-ins in one table — is in Architecture; this section is the practice.

docs.title: How a component reaches the framework
docs.text:
Your component lives in your package (or, on a checkout, a module dropped into opencda_marl/builtin/algorithms/contrib/). It reaches the registry through the same doors an external wheel uses — an opencda_marl.plugins entry point, MARL.plugins in config, or $OPENCDA_MARL_PLUGINS (discovery) — by calling a register_* function at import time:

from opencda_marl.api import register_component

@register_component("planner", "my_planner")
class MyPlanner:
    ...

At startup the framework loads every plugin source once, then freezes the registry — no hot reload, so what ran is exactly what pixi run python -m opencda_marl.plugins lists. A plugin whose declared API version mismatches is rolled back as a unit, across every kind it registered.

docs.title: How the framework picks yours
docs.text: Selection is configuration, never code: each kind has a config key (scenario.traffic.planner.type, agents.agent_type, MARL.components.<kind>, MARL.reward_profile, …— the Architecture table maps all of them). The lifecycle resolves the key through the registry at initialize, so swapping implementations is a one-line profile change.

docs.title: The rules
docs.text:
• Signatures are documented in one place — KIND_SIGNATURES in opencda_marl.api.components states every kind's constructor shape.
  • Replacing an existing key — built-ins included — requires override=True, so nothing is shadowed by a typo.
  • register_component(..., validate=fn) attaches your own config check: a callable over the selecting config block, raising ValueError on a bad configuration. It runs when the framework resolves the component, so a misconfigured plugin fails at initialize with your message instead of deep in the loop.

docs.title: An axis of your own
docs.text:
The registry accepts unknown kinds — a new research axis must not need an engine release. Register under your own kind, resolve it from your own code, and it is listed with everything else:

from opencda_marl.api import register_component
from opencda_marl.api.components import resolve_component


@register_component("curriculum", "linear_demand")
class LinearDemandCurriculum:
    ...

curriculum = resolve_component("curriculum", "linear_demand")()   # your code

docs.title: Verifying a component
docs.text:
The suite's contract tests do not know your component exists, so the check is behavioural, the same as for an algorithm: run a short scenario and read the counters the monitor (or the log) reports — spawns carrying your decisions, the planner's routes actually driven, the reward terms in the episode summaries. For anything that runs on both backends (every kind but agent, which is resolved on CARLA only), the SUMO smoke is the fastest loop:

pixi run python opencda.py -t sumo-marl/intersection/route_rule_path_pcmappo --marl

docs.title: Training Throughput
docs.text: Where the wall-clock goes in a MARL training step, and how to fill a multi-GPU machine. Numbers below were measured on a single-GPU workstation (RTX 5090, ~15 concurrent CAVs, -RenderOffScreen -quality-level=Low) with cProfile attached; treat them as proportions, not absolutes.

docs.title: What one run costs
docs.text:
Backend / learner ms per env step Largest pieces CARLA + MASAC (SAC), 15 CAVs ~60 (profiled) / ~45 unprofiled CARLA physics tick + client reads (~35), learner update (~24: two backward passes, ~500 small kernel launches) SUMO + PCMASAC (SAC), 25 CAVs ~15–20 learner update (~10), observations/rewards/extractor (~5), SUMO step (~0.4) SUMO + PCMAPPO / MAPPO, 25 CAVs ~5–7 acting forward (~2.5), env side; one PPO update per n_steps

Two facts follow from the profiles:

  1. A single run is CPU/launch-bound, not GPU-bound. The networks are small (256-wide MLPs, batch 256, an LSTM over ≤ 30 rows) so the learner update is dominated by kernel-launch latency and Python; the GPU is idle most of the time. One run cannot saturate one large card, let alone two. Faster GPUs barely move the number; more CPU cores and more concurrent runs do.
  2. CARLA is the other half. Even with everything else removed, the physics tick plus the per-step client reads are ~35 ms at 15 CAVs. SUMO steps in well under a millisecond.

docs.title: Filling a multi-GPU box: run cells in parallel
docs.text:
The matrix launcher runs independent cells concurrently, one CARLA server per slot, and spreads learners and servers over the GPUs:

pixi run python scripts/experiments/launch_matrix.py \
    --parallel 8 \
    --cuda-visible-devices 0,1 \
    --carla-gpus 0,1 \
    --carla-rpc-port 2000 \
    ...
  • --cuda-visible-devices 0,1 puts the learner of slot k on GPU k mod 2; --carla-gpus 0,1 starts its CARLA server with -graphicsadapter=k mod 2; with --carla-rpc-port 2000, slot k uses port 2000 + 10*k.
  • Every slot restarts only its own CARLA server (by process handle or by the -carla-rpc-port=<port> marker in the command line), so one slot's failure never takes the others down.
  • Choose --parallel from CPU cores, not VRAM: each slot needs roughly 1.5–2 cores for CARLA plus one for the trainer; a headless CARLA server uses ~1.5–2 GB of VRAM and a learner well under 1 GB, so a large card is never the constraint. Start with cores/3, watch aggregate steps/s, and raise until it stops growing.
  • With many small learner processes on one GPU, NVIDIA MPS (nvidia-cuda-mps-control -d) removes context-switch overhead between them; optional, measure before keeping it.
  • The docker path is equivalent and preferable on shared servers; see Running CARLA in Docker below.
  • SUMO runs need no CARLA at all: they are CPU-bound and can be run in dozens on one machine, each learner sharing a GPU. The launcher is wired to the CARLA momarl/intersection family, so start SUMO profiles directly (pixi run python opencda.py -t sumo-marl/intersection/<profile> --marl), one process per run.
  • At exit the launcher stops the CARLA servers it started (--keep-carla leaves them up); servers that were already listening are never touched.
  • Linux notes: pass --carla-bin /path/to/CarlaUE4.sh when CARLA is not at /opt/CARLA_0.9.16 (the pixi activation default). The launcher strips SDL_VIDEODRIVER from the server's environment — the pixi Linux activation sets it to offscreen for pygame, and UE4's bundled SDL2 exits immediately under it. -graphicsadapter=k follows the Vulkan device order, which matched the CUDA index on the nodes tested.

Measured on a 4-GPU Linux node (CARLA 0.9.16 -RenderOffScreen -quality-level=Low, intersection map, 600-step episodes, --cuda-graph-update):

Concurrent cells ms per env step, MASAC cell Notes 1 10–13 one CARLA server (~2 GB VRAM) + one learner 4 (one per GPU) 12–19 ≈ 2.7–3× the aggregate throughput of one cell

A CARLA server on the intersection map holds ~2.0–2.4 GB of VRAM, so VRAM is never the limit on these cards; CPU cores and the per-slot CARLA tick are. Start-up (CARLA launch + OpenDRIVE world + first spawn) is ~45 s per slot and overlaps across slots.

docs.title: Running CARLA in Docker
docs.text:
--carla-restart-mode docker makes each slot bounce an existing container (docker restart); it never creates one. Start the containers first, one per slot, named by their RPC port — that is the name the launcher restarts:

# One container per slot: port 2000+10k on GPU k.
for k in 0 1 2 3; do
  pixi run python scripts/docker_carla.py start \
      --rpc-port $((2000 + 10 * k)) --streaming-port 0 --gpu $k
done
pixi run python scripts/docker_carla.py status --rpc-port 2000   # or docker ps

Each container runs carlasim/carla:0.9.16 with --network host (so the port is the host port), --gpus device=k, and --restart unless-stopped — CARLA crashes are restarted by docker instead of vanishing the container.

Then run the matrix against them:

pixi run python scripts/experiments/launch_matrix.py \
    --parallel 4 \
    --carla-restart-mode docker \
    --carla-rpc-port 2000 \
    --cuda-visible-devices 0,1,2,3 \
    ...

Notes:

  • Slot k uses port 2000 + 10*k and restarts the container opencda-carla-<port>.
  • Do not pass --carla-gpus in docker mode: --gpus device=k already pins the container to one card, and CARLA sees it as adapter 0.
  • --carla-bin / CARLA_BIN are irrelevant here — no host CARLA install is needed at all.
  • The launcher's exit-time cleanup stops only servers it started itself, so containers survive the run (stop them with scripts/docker_carla.py stop --rpc-port <port>).
  • The account running docker must be in the host's docker group; a permission denied ... /var/run/docker.sock from docker ps means it is not, and no flag in this repo can work around it — use the host-binary path (--carla-restart-mode process --carla-bin /path/to/CarlaUE4.sh) until an administrator adds the account.

docs.title: Per-run speed-ups
docs.text:
• Act on a CPU replica, train on the GPU (<algorithm>.acting_device, default auto). At a dozen agents per step the GPU is launch-bound: a full acting step (context encode, actor, critic, transfers) measures 0.74 ms on the CPU against 1.34 ms on CUDA at these shapes. So with auto a learner that trains on CUDA acts on CPU copies of its actor, critic and context encoder, refreshed after every optimiser step or checkpoint load through one pinned flat copy (0.3 ms), with the value normalisers mirrored. Back-to-back on the same machine state, one SUMO PCMAPPO episode under cProfile: 47–49 s acting on the GPU, 41 s on the replica (the acting path itself 11.5 s → 6.6 s); the update is unaffected. Two caveats. The replica caps torch's intra-op pool (acting_threads, default auto = at most 8): with the default pool of 24 the same step costs 1.45 ms and the run is slower than the GPU. And CPU and GPU arithmetic differ in the last bits, so a run is no longer bit-identical to one that acted on the GPU. acting_device: train keeps acting on the training device.
  • CUDA-graph update for SAC (<algorithm>.cuda_graph_update: true). The tensor-only core of the update (actor/critic/alpha forward + backward
  • optimizer steps, Polyak, metrics) is captured once into a CUDA graph and replayed every update; the data-dependent packed-LSTM encode stays eager and feeds static inputs. Needs CUDA and the frozen encoder (train_context_encoder: false, the default); optimizers become capturable; the graph is re-captured after checkpoint loads and world reloads and the mode falls back to eager on any capture problem. Measured back-to-back: SUMO PCMASAC episode 23.8 → 9.9 ms/step (2.4×), CARLA 1200-step MASAC smoke 73 → 60 s (CARLA physics dominates the rest). No Triton/compiler needed, so it works on Windows and Linux alike; the update it replays is numerically the eager update (equivalence test with a deterministic actor). Off by default — enable it in training configs. One rule: nothing may hold an autograd graph through the SAC actor/critic built outside update() when the graph is captured (every acting path here runs under no_grad, so normal training is fine); if capture fails the learner raises CudaGraphCaptureError rather than continuing, because torch cannot restore the CUDA RNG state in-process afterwards. The same recipe applies to TD3.
  • torch.compile on the acting forward would need Triton (Linux only) and is not wired up.
  • Update-to-data ratio. SAC/TD3 take one gradient step per environment step; each step yields one transition per agent, so the effective ratio is already ~1 gradient step per 15–25 transitions. Fewer gradient steps per env step cut learner time proportionally at the cost of sample efficiency (a hyperparameter trade-off, not a code change); batching several gradient steps into one call does not help, since the cost is per gradient step.
  • What has already been removed: per-transition LSTM forwards at storage time (all learners now store raw neighbour sequences and encode once per update), per-update device syncs, the V2X O(N²) search (no consumer in MARL scenarios), per-spawn map-table construction, per-step metrics assembly with evaluation disabled, and the extra world snapshot per step.
  • Engine-side costs removed before 2.1.0 (one SUMO episode of the bundled example, 2,400 steps, ~14 vehicles, libsumo, under cProfile: 62 → 13 ms/step): the feature extractor walked an OmegaConf mapping per agent per step (31% of the step) and ran three times per step on identical inputs; the neighbour block was a per-ego scalar search with five TTC solves each; a vehicle's population was re-derived per step; the rollout was re-stacked and re-uploaded per PPO epoch. Details in the changelog's Performance section. libsumo must be installed — the engine falls back to TCP TraCI with one warning line and a SUMO step then runs about 13× slower.

docs.title: Measuring
docs.text:
Always compare back-to-back on the same machine state — absolute ms/step drifts by 2–3× with background load — and read the learner's own counters (training_step, updates_performed, buffer size) rather than the episode summary alone: a learner that never acts still produces plausible-looking summaries.

Read the learner's init line too: it names the training device (... device=cuda ...). A torch resolved from PyPI is the CPU build, and a manifest that does not pin PyTorch's own index per platform (as this one does under [target.<platform>.pypi-dependencies]) trains on the CPU without any other sign -- the acting replica then never engages either.

A one-episode profile is the quickest honest measurement. Copy the bundled config root, set max_episodes: 1 in the profile you want to time, and run the CLI under cProfile:

pixi run python -m cProfile -o prof.out -m opencda_marl.cli run -t sumo-marl/intersection/route_speed_only_pcmappo --config-root ./prof_configs

Then read it with pstats sorted by cumulative time. Two checks before trusting a number: the episode summary must be identical to the unprofiled run's (a behaviour-preserving change reproduces the reward bit for bit on the same seed), and unrelated functions must not have moved together — a uniform 1.5–2× inflation across everything is another process on the machine, not the change under test.
